Design for devices that change how patients live.

I’m Jack O’Hearn, a biomedical engineering senior at UVA (materials science minor) targeting mechanical and 3D design roles in medical devices. I’ve modeled structural heart implants, built assistive hardware for ALS patients, and spent a summer in the lab with Medtronic’s cardiac rhythm team watching devices work in real procedures.

Transdermal alcohol feedback bracelet

In development
Role
Design engineer (device and bracelet), two-person team
Stage
Arduino proof of concept
Tools
Arduino, sensor circuit, CAD, DFMA

Problem

Drinkers have no easy way to see how alcohol is affecting them in the moment. We’re building a wrist-worn device that senses alcohol transdermally and gives feedback, aimed at safety, social, and health concerns as wearables go mainstream.

Current work

I’m proving that the sensor can turn ethanol concentration into a usable voltage on an Arduino before we miniaturize. The circuit uses a potentiometric-style front end with bias, divider, and filtering components, shown at left.

Constraints driving the design

  • Sensor size. The sensor, from UK supplier Dart Sensors, sets the minimum footprint of the bracelet.
  • Wearability. It has to look good enough to wear out, or people stop wearing it.
  • Cost. A niche consumer device lives or dies on price.
  • Regulation. It sits near the line of a medical device, so claims and design choices are made carefully.

Vocal Motion: voice-controlled lift chair

Completed, Jan–May 2025
Team
4 students, UVA BME, clinical partner at UVA Health
My role
CAD for the mic mount and electronics enclosure; co-designed the Arduino circuit
Tools
Fusion 360, Prusa 3D printing, Arduino, relays, voice module

Problem

ALS affects over 300,000 people worldwide, and hand atrophy makes standard lift chair remotes hard to use. We built voice control so a patient can raise, recline, and stop the chair without pressing anything.

Design decisions

  • One shot at the integration. Lift chairs are expensive and our budget allowed a single chair. A bad splice on the remote’s wiring could have destroyed it, so we mapped the circuit carefully and drove the chair through relays rather than altering the controller.
  • Weak, slurred speech. The voice system had to stay sensitive enough to recognize degraded speech, so I designed the mic mount to hold the microphone close to the user’s mouth.
  • Reversible by design. The brief forbade irreversible changes to the chair, so everything I designed mounts and removes cleanly.

Results

The chair responds to “up”, “back”, and “pause” by voice. Our bench test log recorded most commands working on the first try, with a few needing two or three. Our clinical partner at UVA Health gave strong feedback at the final presentation.

Medtronic Evolut R frame, rebuilt in CAD

Solo project
Goal
Match the real transcatheter valve frame as closely as possible
Tools
Fusion 360, digital calipers

Challenge

The Evolut R’s self-expanding nitinol frame is a dense, interlaced cell lattice with a narrow waist and flared ends. Modeling it means controlling cell geometry, strut width, and how the pattern wraps around a changing diameter.

Method

I measured the reference frame with calipers, built parametric sketches for the lattice, and patterned them around the axis. The sketches are still in the model tree, so the design can be edited rather than just viewed.

Result

The model matched caliper measurements closely: 45 mm tall, 36.97 mm at the outflow end, 34.09 mm at the inflow end, and a 6.02 mm waist, with the commissure tabs at the top.

Open the CAD model in Fusion

Bifurcating vessel flow simulation

Biotransport course
Inputs
3 L/min inlet, 2.5 cm parent vessel, 1 cm branches, 10 cm total length
Tools
Fusion 360 (geometry), Autodesk CFD, hand calculations

What I did

I modeled a Y-shaped bifurcation in CAD, ran a steady simulation in Autodesk CFD, and checked the results against analytical estimates (maximum velocity as twice the mean for fully developed laminar flow).

SimulatedAnalytical
Parent vessel18.52 cm/s20.37 cm/s
Branch45.89 cm/s63.66 cm/s

Reading the result

The parent vessel agrees within about 10%. The branches differ by about 40%, a gap I’d attribute in part to flow that hasn’t fully developed over the short branch length, and to an unconverged solver at 100 iterations. That’s the first thing I’d test in a follow-up with a longer run and a refined mesh.

Linkage mechanism assembly

Coursework

A Fusion 360 assembly with a slider block riding in a curved slot, a connecting rod, and a rocker arm, all mated to an arched base. Angle and dimension constraints remain in the model, so the motion is driven by the geometry rather than keyframes.
